description: I am an AI engineer who is passionate about AI integration in diverse fields
summary:
Earth Trend Detective is a web app that turns students into data detectives. You ask a question in plain words, such as "Is Arequipa getting warmer?", and five specialists work the case: a coordinator opens it, a scout proposes which Earth-system variables may be trending there, and deterministic code fetches NASA records and tests each hypothesis before an explainer writes a short report.
It answers the challenge's four questions directly: what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is statistically significant. We use NASA POWER monthly data from 1981 to 2025, remove the seasonal cycle, estimate the rate of change with a Theil-Sen slope and 95% confidence interval, and test significance with an autocorrelation-corrected Mann-Kendall test. A map shows the trend in each surrounding grid cell.
No number comes from the AI: it only proposes and explains, so every result is reproducible. This matters because most climate trends are regional, and students need a trustworthy way to test them where they live.
details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Trend Detective answers a question like "Is Arequipa getting warmer?" with

tested evidence. The user types a question, or picks a place and variables on a

map, and the app returns the rate of change, its statistical significance, a

time-series chart and a map of the surrounding region.

Behind the question, five specialists work in a fixed order:

  1. Coordinator (AI): reads the question, identifies the place and declines off-topic requests.
  2. Scout (AI): proposes two to four variables likely to be trending there, with the direction it expects and a physical reason. These are hypotheses, not answers.
  3. Data (code): fetches monthly NASA records and checks their quality.
  4. Statistician (code): tests every hypothesis and analyses each grid cell around the point.
  5. Explainer (AI): writes a short report using only the computed numbers, and says whether each hypothesis held.

Question → Coordinator → Scout → Data → Statistician → Explainer → Report

The key design rule is that no number comes from the AI. The models propose what

to test and explain the result; plain code produces every figure. In our

Arequipa case, the Scout guessed that humidity was falling and the data rejected

it (p = 0.67), which the report states openly.

The statistics

For each series we remove the seasonal cycle (monthly anomalies), estimate the

rate of change with a Theil-Sen slope and 95% confidence interval, and test

significance with a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation (Hamed-Rao).

For the map, we apply false-discovery control because many cells are tested at

once. We calibrated the test on synthetic trendless data: the uncorrected test

raised false alarms in 33 to 52% of strongly autocorrelated series, ours in

about 7%.

Data

NASA POWER monthly records from 1981 to 2025, built on MERRA-2 reanalysis and

CERES satellite radiation: temperature, precipitation, soil wetness, humidity,

wind and sunlight. A client for NASA AppEEARS (MODIS vegetation and land surface

temperature) is included for future use.

Benefits and intended impact

Students and the public can investigate climate change where they live, rather

than reading global averages. Each variable comes with a plain-language

definition, and a toggle shows the raw data with its seasons so users can see

why they must be removed. An "Explore yourself" mode runs the statistics with no

AI, free and in seconds, so classrooms without API budgets can still use it. A

non-significant result is presented as a finding, not a failure.


Tools

Python, LangGraph, Google Gemini, FastAPI, pandas, SciPy and pymannkendall for

the backend; React, TypeScript, Vite and Leaflet for the interface; pytest for

the statistics tests; LangSmith for tracing agent runs.

What makes it creative

We frame analysis as a detective case: the AI forms hypotheses and the data ront

of the user. That models the scientific method instead of presenting AI as an

oracle, and makes "the AI was wrong" a teaching moment.

Factors we considered

  • Trust: numbers must be reproducible, so AI never computes them.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: confidence intervals, p-values and a caution in every report that reanalysis data is not a local weather station and a trend does not prove its cause.
  • False alarms: climate data is autocorrelated, so we measured and corrected the test.
  • Cost and access: the AI is optional, and NASA POWER needs no login.
